drills.coachNote: Your bishop on d4 is only safe because your queen on f6 is defending it along the f6-e5-d4 diagonal — that's the detail Qe6 misses. The instant you offer that queen trade, Bodda_74 takes it: Qxe6 Rxe6, and now nothing guards d4, so Rxd4 just wins the piece clean, with c5 mopping up after. That's the difference between a roughly even middlegame and being down a full bishop for nothing. Instead, c5 keeps the tension and hits b4, so after Bd5 cxb4 axb4 you're trading on your own terms and even winning the exchange with Rxa2 Bxa2. Always check what your queen is quietly holding together before you move her.

drills.title: vs Bodda_74 (684) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Before Bb5, look at your knight on g4 — it's already attacked by the h3 pawn, and with your king on g8, Qxg4+ is a check that wins the knight and gains a tempo at the same time. Bb5 does nothing to fix that: Qxg4+ Kf8, Qh5 keeps hammering, and Bd4 pounces on your knight on c3 too, and you're just bleeding material for nothing. The fix was h5, defending g4 with the pawn on your own terms — even though hxg4 hxg4 trades the knight off, you rip open the h-file toward White's king with f5 and Qg5 next, getting real attacking value instead of losing the piece for free.

drills.coachNote: Your whole edge here is that White's king on h3 is dangerously exposed with your queen sitting right next to it on h5 — that's what's worth 2.8 in your favor despite being down pawns. g6 doesn't add anything to that pressure, and it lets White untangle: Qc4+ shoves your king back to h7, then g4 kicks your queen off h5 entirely, and once she's gone the mating threats evaporate and White's extra pawns just start walking through. Qb5 was the move that kept the initiative alive and denied White's king room to breathe — the line with Kg2 Kf8 Kf2 Qd7 Qc4 shows you steering the game while your king pressure, not White's pawns, stays the deciding factor.

drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here, up material and pressing, and Ne4 throws it away because it walks straight into a fork: Qf5+ is check on your king on h7 while also eyeing the knight on e4 along the f5-e4 diagonal, so after Kh8 is forced, Qxe4 just picks the knight off for free. That single tactic swings the game from winning to losing in one move. Qe8 was the move — it keeps your extra material intact and stays active, and the line Qc2+ Kh8 Qc4 Qe1 Qc8+ shows your queen holding her own and even seizing the initiative with checks of her own. When you're up material in a queen ending, ask what checks are available before you play anything.

When a piece is already hanging, spend the move improving your position or making them pay for it, not marking time.

Ne4 chases the rook away with tempo afterward, but that only wins back time, not the pawn — after Ra3 Rc2 you're simply down material with nothing to show for it. Kd3 was the fix: the king itself guards c3, so even after Bxa6 grabs your a-pawn, you answer with Ra2 and Rxa7, trading pawns evenly instead of losing one outright. drills.coachNote: Your king marched up to g6, and the only thing keeping the mating net closed was your rook on f8 guarding the f7 pawn — Rh8 lets go of that job for nothing. The instant you do, Bxf7# is mate: the bishop on c4 takes the pawn with check, and between your queen on h4 covering g5, h5 and h6, and your knight on g5 covering f7 and h7, your king simply has nowhere to run. That's not a small slip, that's the whole game gone in one move. Nh5 was the move that actually dealt with the danger, forcing the sequence Qxg4 Qxg5 Qxg5+ Kxg5 that gets queens off the board before those attacking pieces can ever combine against you. When your king's this exposed, check what's currently holding the net shut before you touch it.

Meanwhile you still haven't developed your last piece, so White keeps building toward those weak squares while your move accomplished nothing lasting. Nc6 was the move that mattered — it finishes your development and keeps the center solid, and even in lines where White pushes on with Qg3 Nh5 Qg6 Qh4, you're fine because all your pieces are already in the game to meet it, unlike after Bg4 where you're behind in development with real holes near your king.

Rxg3 was the move, because it removes the very pawn holding that mating net together. When your king's this exposed, always check whether your opponent has a mate or check available before spending your move elsewhere.

Now her only real choices are a passive retreat or trading herself off with Qxh2, and Nxh2 recaptures — a full queen for your rook. Qf4 was the move: it threatens Qc7+ along the f4-c7 diagonal, forking the king and the queenside pawns, so Black has to answer with Qd6 to block it. drills.title: vs Mohamed_Behery (840) — Queens Pawn Opening Horwitz Defense
drills.coachNote: Black's king is stuck on e7, boxed in by your knight on f6 and your queen already on g7 — this is exactly the moment to look for checks before grabbing material. Nxh7 forks the rook on f8, but it's not forcing: Black gets a free move, Rd8, to save it, so you only end up a bishop-and-pawn better instead of crushing him. Nd5+ was the real shot — sac the knight, and after exd5 the e-file rips open with Rfe1+, the king gets chased to d6, and Qxf8+ wins the rook outright with check, no time for Black to save it. When the king's this stuck, checks beat grabs — force him before you cash in.

drills.coachNote: You're completely winning here, and there's an actual forced mate on the board: your knight on e6 jumps to f4 with check, and with the king on e2 having nowhere else to go, it's dragged to e3 — from there, your bishop on d5 covers that exact square along the c5 diagonal, so Bc5 is mate. Qxe5+ grabs a pawn with check instead, which feels productive, but it lets White block with Ne4, trade it off, and shuffle the king to safety before castling long. You still win easily from +20, but you swapped a forced mate for a slower grind. When you're this far ahead, look for the check that traps the king, not just any check.

Ne6 is a reasonable developing move, but it's the wrong moment: every tempo you spend improving a piece is a tempo White gets to spend tidying up that king, which is exactly what Qc1 and Ne2 do. Qg3+ keeps the king from ever settling — Ke2 is forced, then Qxe5+ grabs a pawn with another check, chasing him to f2 while you keep landing blows. When the enemy king hasn't castled, checks come before quiet development, even from a winning position.

Qxb7 won a bishop but allowed Qd5 — a queen trade you can't decline (Qxd5 exd5) — and with queens off, the attack on f6 vanished, about five pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs sudharsanee (850) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Variation
drills.coachNote: Your king hunt was working — Black's king is stuck on f6 with nowhere to hide, and you're up nearly nine pawns. Grabbing the bishop with Qxb7 stops the hunt: it lets Qd5 offer a trade, and after Qxd5 exd5 the position simplifies into merely good instead of crushing, with Black's knight later jumping to d2 to harass your rooks. The move was Ne5 — another piece joins the attack. After Ne5 Qg8 Nd7+ Kg5 h4+, the king gets dragged further into the open with every move — you're not just winning material, you're delivering mate. When the enemy king is this exposed, keep hunting before you go shopping for pawns.

drills.explanation: Ne5 puts the knight on a square the d4 pawn protects and attacks the knight on g6. If Nxe5, dxe5+ regains the piece with check, and after Qxe5 your Qf3+ keeps queens on against his airy king. Your Qf3+ instead offered the trade Black wanted: Qxf3 gxf3 killed all the pressure, and Nf4 came next, poking at the h3 pawn.
drills.title: vs sudharsanee (850) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Variation
drills.coachNote: Same idea, but about sequencing. Qf3+ is a real check, but it invites Qxf3 gxf3, trading queens right when you don't want to — you're left with doubled f-pawns and Black's knight jumping to f4, gnawing at your advantage. The fix is just move order: Ne5 first. After Ne5 Nxe5 dxe5+, your pawn recaptures with check, forcing Qxe5 — and now Qf3+ actually works, since Black can't trade it off, only retreat with Kg7, keeping your attack alive with queens still on the board. Before forcing a trade, check whether the same idea works better one move later, with more firepower still in play.

drills.explanation: Both your queen and rook could capture the knight on f4, but Qxf4 is the right way: it wins the knight while the rook on f8 keeps guarding its partner on e8. Rxf4 abandoned that rook — Qxe8+ snapped it off with check, and after Kh7, Qe6 left White completely consolidated. Taking with the wrong piece cost about six pawns.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Before grabbing the knight on f4 with your rook, notice the diagonal from White's queen on h5 — it runs clean through the empty g6 and f7 squares to your rook on e8. The only thing guarding e8 was your other rook on f8, defending along the back rank. The moment you played Rxf4 with that rook, e8 lost its defender, and Qxe8+ just wins your rook for free, turning a roughly equal game into a disaster. Qxf4 was right there instead — same knight, same pawn win, but your queen does the capturing, your rook stays on f8 guarding e8, and the position stays balanced heading toward Qe2 and a fair trade on f4 later.

drills.explanation: a6 strikes at White's overextended queenside: after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook enters the game down the a-file, and b5 is met calmly by Ra8. Castling let White play Qe2, hitting your knight on c4 — a piece with no defenders — and you had to scramble with c6 and b5 just to hold it, leaving White a wedge pawn on c6.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: White's pawns on b4 and b5 look imposing but b5 isn't actually defended yet — that's why a6 was calling to be played, hitting it immediately. After bxa6 Rxa6 your rook lands on an open a-file with real activity, and if b4 pushes to b5 again you just retreat to a8 having gained time. Castling instead handed White a free tempo: Qe2 goes up, the position consolidates, and the later break in the center starts working in White's favor instead of yours, costing you the edge you had. Your knight on c4 is a great outpost, but outposts need follow-up — strike at the base of the pawn chain before your opponent gets to organize.

drills.explanation: You were a full piece up and just needed to consolidate. c5 gains space, and the knight calmly reroutes to c6 next with b6 and normal development to follow. Ng4 put the knight on a square covered by White's queen all the way back on d1 — Qxg4 took it for nothing, handing the extra piece straight back.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Your knight jump to g4 ran straight into White's queen on d1 — d1 to g4 is a wide-open diagonal, and nothing of yours covers g4 to punish the capture. Qxg4 just wins the piece outright, no trick needed, and you're down a full knight for nothing — a 4.5 pawn swing from a roughly equal game. The engine wanted c5 instead, a quiet pawn push grabbing central space and prepping Nc6, keeping things calm and balanced. Before sending a knight into open territory, scan the diagonals and files behind it first — a queen sitting on the back rank sees further than it looks.

drills.explanation: Bxa2 trades off White's light-squared bishop on your terms: after Rxa2 you swing rooks to the e-file with Rae8 and Re6, sitting solidly behind the e5 pawn. Rad8 left the bishops eyeballing each other one move too long — Bh6 came with threats at your king, and after g6, Bxe6 fxe6 left you with doubled, weak e-pawns.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on e6 sits on a completely open diagonal back to a2 — nothing in between — and White's bishop sits right there on the other end. That trade is yours to take: Bxa2 right now. Play the quiet Rad8 instead and you hand White the initiative on that same diagonal — Bh6 comes first, hitting g7 and forcing the weakening g6, and only then does White swap on e6 with Bxe6, so the same trade happens but on White's terms instead of yours. You were winning by over four pawns and gave back a chunk of it just by not grabbing the free bishop while it was sitting there.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your knight had just landed a monster idea on c6 — from there it forks Black's queen on e7 and rook on d8 at once. Nxc6 wins material outright: Qd6 moves the queen away, Nxd8 grabs the rook, Qxd8 recaptures, and you're up a full exchange with Qxg5 mopping up another pawn. Instead a4 wandered off to the other wing and let the moment pass — Black immediately traded off your knight with Nxe5, and after Qxe5 Ne4 the other knight jumped in with tempo, clawing back most of your 4.8 pawn edge. When a knight lands on a square hitting two pieces at once, finish the fork before looking anywhere else on the board.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Both your knights are hitting pieces here, but the one on e5 is only defended by your d4 pawn, because Black's knight on e4 blocks your queen from backing it up along the e-file. b5 ignores that completely — Black just plays Nxe5, and after bxa6 bxa6 your other knight has to slink back to b3. You've dropped a full piece for nothing. Nxc6! was sitting right there instead: your e5 knight grabs the c6 knight, and after bxc6 Qd3 you're hitting that same e4 knight again, forcing it to trade itself off via Nxc5 bxc5 while Black's queenside pawns get wrecked. Before opening lines with a pawn push, always check your own pieces are still safe first.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: You're completely winning here — Rxf7! grabs the pawn shielding Black's king and sets up a forced mate: Re2, Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8#. Instead you played Qg5, and that let Black play Rxf2, because with your g-pawn already pushed to g4, the g2 square is empty and your king on g1 has nothing left guarding it. After Qe5 and Rf3, Black's rook is marching to f1 and you've gone from delivering mate to defending your own king. When you're this far ahead, the question isn't 'what's a good move,' it's 'what finishes the attack right now' — a slower move just hands the opponent time to create threats of their own.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Look at Black's rook on c8 — nothing defends it, not the rook on f8, not the king on g8. Qxc8! just wins it outright, and after Qb5 Re8 Qf1+ Rxf1 h5 you're cleaning up an already-won position. Instead you played Qd5, which does nothing about that hanging rook, and it gave Black's queen a free run — Qxa3, then after you grab d4, Qxh3, and suddenly that queen is prowling right next to your own king, needing R7e3 just to hold things together. Before deciding where to put a piece, always scan for anything of the opponent's that's simply hanging first — that check comes before everything else.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Bf5+ feels like a free check, but it walks straight into e6, which hits your bishop and forces it all the way back to c2. While you're retreating, Black's pawn on g5 just takes your other bishop on f4 with gxf4 — you checked with one piece and lost the other for nothing. Nxg5! was the real move: after fxg5 Bxg5 you've traded a knight for a pawn but ripped open Black's kingside, and your bishop on g5 eyes f6 while Black's pieces trip over each other with Nf6 Qf3 Nb8. Before throwing in a check, ask what it actually threatens — one that just gets met and costs you a piece isn't progress.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Same trap here — Bf5+ doesn't fix your real problem, which is that your bishop on f4 sits on the same diagonal as Black's pawn on g5. After e6 hits your checking bishop, you retreat to c2, and gxf4 just wins your other bishop for a pawn — a tempo spent checking, and you come out a full piece down. The engine wants e4, striking the center where you already have a space edge: after gxf4 exd5 you open lines, and even Na7 Qa4+ c6 forces Black's pieces onto awkward squares while you're ahead in development. A 'free' check only helps if it doesn't leave something else hanging — here it left f4 wide open.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight jumping to g5 walks straight onto the c1-g5 diagonal, which is completely open — Bxg5 just wins the piece for nothing, no compensation at all. After f6, trying to trap the bishop, White simply plays Nxe5 and grabs your e5 pawn too, so now you're down a full piece and a pawn. Nd6 was the move — pulling the knight back to safety, eyeing c4 and f5 — and after Rxe5+ Be7 Qe2 you're only down the e5 pawn, which is standard in this Berlin structure, nothing more. Before jumping a piece forward, always check every diagonal the opponent's minor pieces control — c1 to g5 was a wide-open highway.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight is still sitting on g5, still on that same open diagonal from the bishop on c1 — playing Be7 does nothing to rescue it, so White just plays Bxg5 and finally cashes in the piece you left hanging last move. After Be6 Bxe7 Qxe7 the bishops trade off, but you're still down a full knight from g5 with nothing to show for it. Ne6 was the fix — hopping the knight off that diagonal to a safe, central square — and after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 Qd5 the position stays roughly balanced instead of you being down material. When a piece is hanging, deal with it before playing any other move, even a natural one like Be7.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on f4 has a clean shot at Black's queen on d8 — Bc7! hits it directly, forces it to move, and after Qd7 you follow with b6, reroute your knight from b3 to the outpost on c6, and lift your rook to a4, building real pressure while Black scrambles to defend. Playing e4 first just hands Black a free move: he plays Bd7, and by the time you get to Bc7, he calmly parks the queen on c8 and the whole plan is defused. When you spot a move that gains a tempo by hitting the queen, play it immediately rather than a 'natural' move like e4 — every extra move you give the opponent is a move to fix the problem you were about to create.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: You had a roughly balanced position, but Qc3 misses what Black's bishop wants to do next. After ...Bd7, that bishop swings onto the c8-h3 diagonal aiming straight at your pawn on b5 — with your queen off on c3, nothing guards it anymore, so ...Bxb5 just wins the pawn clean, and Rfb1 leaves you regrouping down material instead of level. The move was Qc5: it jumps forward and hits Black's queen on b6. After ...Qd8 retreats, Bd6 attacks the loose knight on e7, and after ...Re8 Bxe7 Rxe7 you've won the piece. Before parking your queen, check what diagonal you just vacated.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were up a mountain of material here, but Nb7 walks right past the winning shot and hangs your own knight instead. Your knight on d6 had a check on f5 that forks the White king on g3 and the rook on g7 — that's Nf5+. Instead, after ...Nb7, White plays Rc7+, and once your king steps to d8 the rook just scoops the knight off b7 next move with Rxb7, handing back the edge you'd built. Nf5+ Kf4 Nxg7 wins the rook outright, and after ...Ke5 Nh5 the knight tucks away safely while your c-pawn rolls forward. Whenever your king can check, ask what else that same move attacks.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning, up more than six points, but Rd7 drops the rook for nothing — the d-file between your rook and White's rook on d1 is wide open, so Rxd7 just wins it outright, no strings attached. Even the follow-up ...Bd6 doesn't help: White plays bxc6, grabbing your knight too, and you're left recapturing ...bxc6 having lost a rook and a knight in a position you were dominating. The move was Bxg3+, your bishop on f4 grabbing the pawn on g3 with check — after Kxg3, White's rook on d1 is left totally undefended, so Rxd1 wins it clean. A free check that opens a file is worth more than any quiet move.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: This is the kind of moment where you had a forced mate on the board and grabbed a pawn instead. Black's queen is still home on d8, the king is stuck on e7, and your knight on f6 is smothering the escape squares — Qxb7+ forces ...Qc7 as the only block, and Qxc7 is then mate, since your queen covers d6 and d8 while the knight on f6 covers e8. Instead exd4 let the position continue with ...Bg7, dxc5, Qc7, Rd7+ — still winning for you, but you gave the king a chance to breathe instead of ending it on the spot. When the enemy king is this boxed in, look for forcing checks before any capture, even a free pawn.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You're still crushing here, but Nd7 only looks like a fork — Black just plays Bg7, tucks the bishop away, and you've spent a move winning nothing, since the 'forked' rook on b8 was never actually stuck. The real shot was Rd7+: your rook checks the king on e7, and because the only reply is ...Qxd7 with the queen, your knight on f6 recaptures with Nxd7 — you've just traded a rook for Black's queen, a far bigger haul than a cosmetic fork. Before playing a fork, ask whether the forked piece can simply step aside; a check that forces a capture beats a fork the opponent can just walk away from.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: You were already worse here, but Qh4 hangs the queen outright — Black's queen on e7 sits on the same e7-h4 diagonal, and with f6 and g5 both empty, ...Qxh4 just wins your queen for free and the game's essentially over. The safe square was Qa3, keeping the queen off that diagonal while still eyeing the queenside; after ...Re8 c4 d4 g4 you're still fighting uphill, but at least you're not down a whole queen. Before moving your queen anywhere, trace every diagonal and file running through the target square — that one check would've saved you here.
